items.prompt: Why does a binary search tree make a poor index for data stored on disk?
hints: Think about what happens each time the search moves down one level.
Data on disk is read one block at a time, and each node visited can mean another block read.
A balanced BST with a million keys is about 20 levels deep, so a search may need about 20 slow disk reads.

options.text: Each level can mean another slow disk read, and it needs about 20 levels for a million keys
options.feedback: Right. The problem is depth: every level visited can cost a block read.

options.text: Its keys are not kept in any order
options.feedback: A BST does keep its keys ordered: smaller left, larger right. The problem is how deep it gets.

options.text: Comparing two keys takes longer than reading from disk
options.feedback: It is the other way round. A comparison in memory is far faster than reading a block from disk.

items.prompt: How big is one B-tree node usually made?
hints: What does the disk hand over in a single read?
A disk always reads a whole block, so a node should make use of all of it.
Each node is sized to one disk block (page), so one read brings in a whole node of keys.

options.text: About one disk block, holding many keys
options.feedback: Yes. One read brings in a whole node, so each read does as much work as possible.

options.text: One key, like a node in a binary search tree
options.feedback: Then every key would cost a separate disk read. B-trees pack many keys per node.

options.text: As big as the whole file
options.feedback: Then the whole file would be read for every search, which is exactly what an index avoids.

items.prompt: Each B-tree node has up to 100 children. About how many levels does the tree need for 1 000 000 keys?
hints: Each level multiplies the number of nodes by up to 100.
Count how many keys 1, 2, 3 levels can hold when every node has 100 children.
100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000, so 3 full levels hold just under a million keys: about 4 levels. A balanced BST needs about 20.

options.feedback: Right. With 100 children per node, every level multiplies the reach by 100, so a few levels cover a million keys.
That is the height of a balanced binary tree. With 100 children per node the tree is far shorter.
That would be a very tall tree. Each level multiplies the number of keys reachable by up to 100.

items.prompt: When a B-tree lives on disk, what mostly decides how fast a search is?
hints: Which is slower: work in memory, or fetching from disk?
Comparisons inside a node happen in memory once the node has been read.
The number of nodes read from disk, which is one per level, dominates the cost.

options.text: How many nodes (disk blocks) it reads
options.feedback: Yes. Each node read is a slow disk access, and the search reads one node per level.

options.text: How many keys it compares inside each node
options.feedback: Those comparisons happen in fast memory once the node is loaded. The disk reads dominate.

options.text: How many keys the whole tree holds
options.feedback: More keys matter only a little: the height grows logarithmically, so reads grow very slowly.
